slot.brief: A wire stretched by known amount with a hanging mass; use Y = stress/strain to find elongation or the maximum load for a given breaking stress.

stem: A wire of length $2\ \text{m}$ stretches by $1\ \text{mm}$ when a mass of $5\ \text{kg}$ is suspended from it. The Young's modulus and breaking stress of the wire are $2 \times 10^{11}\ \text{N m}^{-2}$ and $4 \times 10^8\ \text{N m}^{-2}$, respectively. The maximum mass that can be suspended from the wire without breaking it is (take $g = 10\ \text{m s}^{-2}$)

verdicts.working: Area from stretch data: A = FL/(YΔL) = (50×2)/(2×10¹¹×10⁻³) = 5×10⁻⁷ m². Breaking force = σA = 4×10⁸×5×10⁻⁷ = 200 N ⇒ M = 200/10 = 20 kg.

working:
Step 1: Calculate the longitudinal strain under the initial load:
$$\varepsilon = \dfrac{\Delta L}{L} = \dfrac{1 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}}{2\ \text{m}} = 5 \times 10^{-4}$$

Step 2: Calculate the tensile stress $\sigma_1$ produced by the mass $m_1 = 5\ \text{kg}$:
$$\sigma_1 = Y \varepsilon = (2 \times 10^{11}\ \text{N m}^{-2}) \times (5 \times 10^{-4}) = 1.0 \times 10^8\ \text{N m}^{-2}$$

Step 3: Relate stress to the suspended mass. Since stress is directly proportional to the applied load ($\sigma = \dfrac{m g}{A}$):
$$\dfrac{M_{\max}}{m_1} = \dfrac{\sigma_{\text{break}}}{\sigma_1}$$
$$M_{\max} = 5\ \text{kg} \times \dfrac{4 \times 10^8\ \text{N m}^{-2}}{1.0 \times 10^8\ \text{N m}^{-2}} = 5 \times 4 = 20\ \text{kg}$$

draft.distractor_notes: Option A encodes forgetting the original length $L = 2\ \text{m}$ when computing strain (taking strain as $\Delta L = 10^{-3}$), which doubles $\sigma_1$ to $2 \times 10^8\ \text{N m}^{-2}$ and yields $M = 10\ \text{kg}$.
